newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sabena confirms deal with Virgin.
newsitem.headline: Sabena confirms deal with Virgin.

text.p: Belgian national carrier Sabena said on Friday it signed an agreement with Richard Branson's Virgin Express regional airline for flights between Brussels and London Heathrow.

Virgin Express had prematurely advertised in some Belgian newspapers on Thursday it was offering nine flights a day to London although a deal between the two carriers had not yet been reached due to last-minute hiccups in talks.
"From October 27, Sabena and Virgin Express will jointly operate the Brussels-London/Heathrow line," Sabena said in a statement.
Sabena chief executive Paul Reutlinger said the agreement enabled the loss-making Belgian airline, owned 49.5 percent by Swissair, to further expand its European network.

Sabena said the nine flights to Heathrow would be operated by Virgin Express with Boeing 737-300 planes, which allowed Sabena to use three Boeing 737 for longer-distance flights to cities such as Helsinki, Venice and Bilbao.

The deal gives Virgin Express access to coveted take-off and landing slots at Heathrow. It will also enable it to offer connections via Brussels between London and seven continental European cities served by Virgin Express.
Sabena said it was already handling technical maintenance of Virgin Express planes but will now also take care of ground handling for Virgin Express at Brussels' Zaventem airport.

Sabena Catering will provide meals for the new Express Business Class in which business travellers can travel up to 50 percent cheaper. Economy Class will now have only a restricted 'no frills' service.
Sabena, owned 49.5 percent by Swissair had a 1995 group loss before provisions of 530 million Belgian francs.
The deal with Virgin Express, launched in April after Branson bought 90 percent of EuroBelgian Airlines SA (EBA), is seen by analysts as part of its drive to return to profit.
Reutlinger has said Sabena needed to make extra savings of 4.7 billion francs ($150 million), including two billion francs in labour-related cost reductions between now and 1998.
Talks with unions on Reutlinger's plan started in June and are due to end by the end of this month.
Sabena's announcement earlier this month it had a two billion Belgian francs loss in the first half of 1996 further raised pressure on unions, analysts said.
As part of the plan, Sabena has already sold its cargo capacity to Swissair's cargo division.
